newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia says hopes U.S. legislator's bill fails.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia says hopes U.S. legislator's bill fails.

text.p: Indonesia said on Wednesday the views of a U.S. congressman seeking to cut off aid from the United States were not representative and expressed hope that the move would fail.
"We don't believe the views of Representative Patrick Kennedy represent the views of the American people or the government," Indonesian Foreign Ministry spokesman Ghaffar Fadyl told Reuters.
On Tuesday, Kennedy's spokesman said the congressman planned to introduce a bill on March 17 to cut off U.S. aid to Indonesia because of violations of human rights in East Timor.
Fadyl said the views of Kennedy, who visited East Timor for two days last December, were exaggerated and distorted, and that he was politicking to boost his local electoral appeal.
"We hope that it (the proposed bill) will not get enough support," Fadyl said.

U.S. companies were concerned that the Rhode Island Democrat wanted to impose trade sanctions against Indonesia. But his spokesman, Larry Berman, said Kennedy was targeting military and economic aid, not trade.
"What we are more interested in doing is sending a message to the government of Indonesia," Berman said. "We want to get Indonesia to stop abusing human rights."
The U.S. State Department and Amnesty International have listed several cases of human rights violations in East Timor.

Washington provides about $50 million in annual economic assistance to Indonesia for health, environment, anti-poverty, and regulatory programmes. It also sends about $600,000 in assistance for military training, according to U.S. officials.
Trade between the United States and Indonesia totals about $6 billion annually.
The U.S. state of Massachusetts is debating its own legislation to bar companies that do business in Indonesia from doing business with the state.

Indonesia invaded East Timor in 1975. Jakarta still faces some armed and political opposition to its rule in the former Portuguese colony, which it formally annexed in 1976. The United Nations has never recognised Indonesia's rule of East Timor.
